title: How the UAE Financed a Plan to Smear American Muslims
author: Emran Feroz

A private intelligence firm working for the United Arab Emirates commissioned
a report on American Muslim organizations from a U.S. researcher as part of a
campaign aimed at damaging their reputations with allegations of links to the
Muslim Brotherhood, according to an archive of leaked documents obtained by
Drop Site News.

The commission from the Geneva-based firm Alp Services resulted in a 2018
report produced by Lorenzo Vidino, the author of several books on the Muslim
Brotherhood and head of the George Washington Program on Extremism at George
Washington University. That report and other documents included in the archive
lay out a proposed campaign against Muslim organizations in the United States,
aspects of which appear to be ongoing.

Titled "The MB in the US," Vidino's report lists the names of dozens of Muslim
Americans and civil society groups that he claims are part of a vast and
secretive extremist network in the U.S.--including the Council on American-
Islamic Relations (CAIR), the Islamic Society of North America (ISNA), the
Muslim Public Affairs Council (MPAC), the Muslim American Society (MAS), the
U.S. Council of Muslim Organizations, the charity Islamic Relief USA, along
with several organizations, mosques, and individually named activists and
religious leaders.

The report does not provide evidence to substantiate Vidino's allegations. But
it effectively created a blacklist of Muslim American organizations and
individuals that could be used to damage their reputations with allegations of
association with the Muslim Brotherhood, amid an ongoing effort pushed forward
in part by the UAE to have the U.S. designate the group as a terrorist
organization.

Lorenzo Vidino and Alp Services did not respond to requests for comment. The
UAE's Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not respond to questions.

The broad effort to tie American Muslim groups to the Muslim Brotherhood has
continued in the years since Vidino's report for Alp Services. On August 5,
2026, a Senate Judiciary subcommittee convened a
[hearing](https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/committee-activity/hearings/hidden-
in-plain-sight-confronting-the-muslim-brotherhood-network-in-
america-08-05-2026) titled "Hidden in Plain Sight: Confronting the Muslim
Brotherhood Network in America." One of the three witnesses was Lara Burns, a
senior research fellow at Vidino's Program on Extremism, who described CAIR,
ISNA, the North American Islamic Trust and the Muslim Students Association as
components of a covert Brotherhood and Hamas infrastructure, while citing
Vidino's published work in portions of her written testimony.

## A Covert Defamation Campaign

The UAE has been a major advocate of designating the Brotherhood as a
terrorist group in Western countries after the organization won elections in
several countries following the 2011 Arab Spring, leading to a perception that
it was a threat to the power of the monarchy in Abu Dhabi. That campaign has
gradually grown into a broader effort to target political rivals, or even
individuals merely seen as suspicious or hostile by the Emirates.

The documents contained in the archive, which was provided by the reporting
consortium European Investigative Collaborations, reveal how the smear
campaign was intended to come together.

An internal Alp planning memo from July 2017 proposed creating, with Vidino's
help, a "cartography" of alleged Muslim Brotherhood and Qatari influence
networks in both the U.S. and Europe. That proposed map would encompass
charities, lobbyists, media outlets, academics, political supporters, banks,
investors, and businesspeople. Alp also contemplated deeper investigations
intended to uncover what it called "red flags"--a reference to finding
negative personal or professional information and rumors about selected
targets.

In February 2018, Alp secured approval for an operation code-named "Arnica 6"
that would ultimately turn some of the investigations into covert reputational
and financial pressure campaigns. The action plan proposed hostile media
placements, providing unattributed briefings to trusted journalists, negative
Wikipedia editing about targets, submissions of derogatory information to
regulatory compliance databases, and discreet political lobbying.

Some details of Alp's European activities on behalf of the UAE were previously
[reported](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2023/04/03/the-dirty-secrets-of-
a-smear-campaign) by the New Yorker, which described efforts to target a
commodities trader named Hazim Nada, as well as Muslim organizations in
Europe. The accusation of association with the Muslim Brotherhood, spread by
Alp Services through anonymously posted online articles and Wikipedia entries,
ruined Nada's business and reputation while generating millions of euros in
revenue for the firm.

The New Yorker noted that Mario Brero, the head of Alp Services, whose primary
client on the project was an Emirati research institution reporting to UAE
leader Mohammed bin Zayed, asked Vidino to find "'interesting
elements/rumours' on the other side of the Atlantic," but did not provide
specifics on any follow-up efforts to identify or target Americans or
U.S.-based organizations.

On May 12, 2018, Vidino transmitted a series of documents to Alp over
WhatsApp, including his report on the Muslim Brotherhood in America and
supporting memos on Muslim organizations in Chicago and groups linked to the
Turkish government.

The Brotherhood report was sent as a Microsoft Word file that includes
metadata indicating that Vidino was the author. Other documents suggest that
the proposed fee for producing this report was 2,000 euros.

The report mapped a wide swath of Muslim American civic life, including
registered, well-established organizations that he claimed comprised a covert
Muslim Brotherhood network in America.

Vidino did not provide evidence that the listed individuals or organizations
were part of the Muslim Brotherhood or any other transnational organization,
but asserted they were "spawns" of the movement and represented its "centers
of gravity" in the United States.

By July 2018, Alp had transformed Vidino's material into a polished report
intended for its client, an Emirati entity called ARIAF Studies and Research
LLC. Alp also assembled a separate package of documents for an August 8
meeting with Matar Humaid al-Neyadi, an Emirati official who appears elsewhere
in the archive as the client contact for Arnica and currently serves as the
UAE's ambassador to Kuwait. Al-Neyadi did not respond to a request for
comment.

## Targeting Civil Society Groups

Prior to joining the GWU program, Vidino worked worked for the Investigative
Project on Terrorism, a research organization founded by Steve Emerson, a
controversial "terrorism expert" who has been accused of spying on American
Muslim organizations and falsely claiming that major cities in Europe had
become "no-go zones" under the control of Muslim immigrants. Vidino has
remained influential as an expert commentator in the United States.

In a Wall Street Journal op-ed in early August, Vidino
[wrote](https://www.wsj.com/opinion/the-islamist-threat-isnt-only-
terrorism-4a8d8ff2?mod=e2two) that the Trump administration must begin
targeting what he referred to as non-violent "Islamist" groups, claiming that
such groups were already operating in "politics, education and grassroots
activism," and that "Islamist actors are funding politically aligned
candidates in U.S. elections nationwide." The article did not provide any
evidence for the claims or specify what it defined as "Islamist actors."

A previous target of Vidino and Alp Services in Europe was an Austrian scholar
now living in the U.S. named Farid Hafez. After rumors of his association with
the Brotherhood were spread by Alp and later shared with Austria's
intelligence services, Hafez's home was raided by Austrian police in November
2020. He was later cleared of any wrongdoing and the operations themselves
were later found to be unlawful by Austrian courts.

"Vidino never really says something specific like this person is a Muslim
Brotherhood person, but instead uses the strategy of saying that those people
have a relationship with other people who themselves have a relationship to
the Brotherhood," said Hafez, who added that Vidino's reports predominantly
relied on secondary sources. "There was never really a clear statement that
someone could nail him down over in a courtroom, because he never really said
anything too specific in his accusations, and that was really the strategy."

Vidino's report for Alp claimed that despite having no visible organizational
structure, the Muslim Brotherhood's American branch is "arguably one of the
largest and best organized in the West," claiming that it had established
itself with the arrival of Muslim college students to the country in the 1960s
and has continued expanding its influence through a web of connected
political, financial, and educational organizations.

In addition to laying out the names and personnel associated with the largest
and most well-known Muslim organizations in the U.S., the report also sets the
stage for a broader possible crackdown on mosques in general by targeting an
organization called the North American Islamic Trust, which holds the deeds to
hundreds of American mosques.

A short section devoted to charities also lists a number of charity
organizations including Islamic Relief USA, the Zakat Foundation of America,
Life for Relief and Development and Anera, a group that helps refugees in
Palestine, Lebanon, and Jordan.

Islamic Relief, a UK-headquartered charity that operates in disaster zones
around the world, was also the target of a separate campaign funded by the
UAE, code-named "Crocus," which was aimed at associating the organization with
an American Muslim scholar named Yasir Qadhi, according to the documents.

The documents in the archive from Alp related to the Crocus campaign cite a
number of British press reports about Qadhi from 2017, quoting his past
statements about Islamic criminal punishments, homosexuality, and Shia
Muslims; describing him as a "radical preacher"; and noting that some of his
social media posts had been shared by Islamic Relief employees. Qadhi had
previously renounced some of his earlier views and has been defended by the
charity as an opponent of terrorism. Islamic Relief has continued to be
regularly targeted by social media campaigns led by UAE-backed online
influencers.

The report on American Muslims supplied by Vidino also included a section on
alleged Turkish government influence in the U.S., including ties between
Turkish officials and several American Muslim organizations and individuals.
The Turkish government has also been a rival of the UAE in recent years after
the two countries found themselves on opposite sides of the Arab Spring.

American Muslim activists who were named by Vidino denied the accusations
contained in the dossier, describing them as political attacks aimed at trying
to exclude them from political life.

"These are tactics that have been used against us for all these years to
marginalize us and exclude us from politics. They are worried about losing
their grip and monopolizing the American political scene," said Salam Al-
Marayati, president and co-founder of the Muslim Public Affairs Council
(MPAC). "If they can't win the argument--which they lose every time,
particularly on foreign policy--their reaction is that these are wolves in
sheep's clothing, this is a Trojan horse, we are the Muslim Brotherhood."

## Extremist Accusations

For her August appearance before the Senate Judiciary subcommittee hearing on
the Muslim Brotherhood, Laura Burns submitted written testimony describing
CAIR, ISNA, the North American Islamic Trust, and the Muslim Students
Association as components of a covert Brotherhood and Hamas infrastructure.

Another witness, Arielle Klepach of the National Jewish Advocacy Center,
accused a still wider network that included CAIR, ICNA, ISNA, MAS, MSA and
NAIT of being secret extremist groups and cited a series of Vidino's published
reports. Klepach urged lawmakers to use financial and legal pressure against
CAIR in particular, pointing to bills to strip the organization of its tax-
exempt status, designate it as a terrorist organization, and investigate its
alleged foreign ties.

Other efforts to crack down on Muslim participation in American public life
have included proposed legislation and executive orders. A bill called the
Muslim Brotherhood Terrorist Designation Act, sponsored by Rep. Mario Diaz-
Balart (R-Fla.) and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) would require annual government
reports identifying Brotherhood branches and evaluating them for terrorist
designation and sanctions. A separate bill introduced by Rep. Chip Roy
(R-Texas) would designate CAIR as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist
Organization, freeze its assets, revoke its tax exemption and prohibit
Americans from dealing with it.

In November 2025, Trump signed an executive order directing the State and
Treasury departments to [begin](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-
sheets/2025/11/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-begins-process-to-
designate-certain-muslim-brotherhood-chapters-as-foreign-terrorist-
organizations-and-specially-designated-global-terrorists/) the process of
designating certain Muslim Brotherhood branches, including those in Egypt,
Jordan, and Lebanon, as terrorist organizations.

That same month, Texas Governor Greg Abbott issued a proclamation to designate
both CAIR and the Muslim Brotherhood as foreign terrorist and transnational
criminal organizations and said the designation would prohibit them and their
alleged affiliates from acquiring land in Texas. Gov. Ron DeSantis
[announced](https://x.com/RonDeSantis/status/2104951116077191236) on September
29 that Florida had officially designated the Muslim Brotherhood, CAIR, and
"antifa" as terrorist organizations.

These efforts have continued to be supported not only by pro-Israel
organizations, but also Emirati officials who have pressed forward with an
ambitious strategy of using their influence in the U.S. and Europe to wield
terrorism accusations against their political rivals, using alleged ties to
the Brotherhood as a preferred tactic. In January 2026, its foreign ministry
welcomed the Trump administration's designation of Brotherhood branches in
Egypt, Jordan, and Lebanon, while Roy's proposed legislation against CAIR
explicitly cites the UAE's own 2014 designation of the organization.

"The unfortunate fact is that the UAE has come to play a destabilizing role in
the Middle East and in relation to Arab and Muslim communities in the West,"
said Osama Abu Irshaid, national director for American Muslims for Palestine,
who is also named along with his organization in the Vidino and Alp documents.
"They are not doing it because they truly believe we are an extension of the
Muslim Brotherhood in the U.S. or EU, but because they feel that their
interests are threatened, because we calling for freedom and liberty and are
succeeding in our aspirations for integration, and they fear this may one day
translate into foreign policy pressure on them to cease their repression
across the the region."

"There is nothing that would substantiate their claims. We are American
organizations, we are American citizens, and we have the right to come
together to organize politically. Everything we are doing is in public and
there are no secrets," Irshaid added. "They want to demonize us and derail our
agenda, but the claim that we are part of a grand conspiracy is simply a big
lie."
